evidence: This is supported by citations to Fay and Benavides, 2005 and Schacherer et al., 2009.

claim: Wine strains from Europe, Australia, Chile and New Zealand share recent ancestry and reflect human migration history.
source: These strains do not strictly follow geographic boundaries, for example, wine strains from Europe, Australia, Chile and New Zealand share recent ancestry and reflect human migration history (Legras et al., 2007; Liti et al., 2009; Goddard et al., 2010; Dunn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Legras et al., 2007; Liti et al., 2009; Goddard et al., 2010; Dunn et al., 2012.

claim: Some S. cerevisiae lineages are not associated with human activity and appear to be characteristic of the geographic area.
source: Other lineages are not associated with human activity and appear to be characteristic of the geographic area.
evidence: This is based on data from population genomics studies.

claim: Oak strains from woodlands in North America are characteristic of the geographic area.
source: These include oak strains from woodlands in North America and bertam palm strains from the Malaysian rainforest.
evidence: This is based on data from field surveys and genomic analysis.

claim: Bertam palm strains from the Malaysian rainforest are characteristic of the geographic area.
source: These include oak strains from woodlands in North America and bertam palm strains from the Malaysian rainforest.
evidence: This is based on data from field surveys and genomic analysis.

claim: The Malaysian lineage has the peculiarity of being reproductively isolated from all other lineages due to a complex series of chromosomal rearrangements.
source: The Malaysian lineage has the peculiarity of being reproductively isolated from all other lineages due to a complex series of chromosomal rearrangements (Cubillos et al., 2011; Marie-Nelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cubillos et al., 2011 and Marie-Nelly et al., 2014.

claim: Chinese isolates of S. cerevisiae appear to exhibit strong population structure.
source: Although full genome information is not yet available for Chinese isolates of S. cerevisiae, they appear to exhibit strong population structure, with essentially double the combined amount of genetic variation identified in S. cerevisiae isolates sampled from the rest of the world (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Chinese isolates from primeval forests fall into ancient and remarkably diverged lineages.
source: Chinese isolates from primeval forests fall into ancient and remarkably diverged lineages (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on data from population genomics studies, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: China harbours a reservoir of S. cerevisiae natural genetic variation, which perhaps gives an indication as to where the species originated.
source: These results suggest that China harbours a reservoir of S. cerevisiae natural genetic variation, which perhaps gives an indication as to where the species originated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic diversity data from Chinese isolates.

claim: Far East Asia is the only region where all the Saccharomyces sensu stricto species have been isolated.
source: This enrichment of genetic diversity is not limited to S. cerevisiae intra-species variation as Far East Asia is also the only region where all the Saccharomyces sensu stricto species have been isolated.
evidence: This is based on data from field surveys and species distribution.

claim: Many S. cerevisiae strains have been found to have mosaic recombinant genomes, which reflect a mixed ancestry likely originating from outcrosses between genetically distinct lineages.
source: In addition to these distinct lineages, many S. cerevisiae strains have been found, after sequencing, to have mosaic recombinant genomes, which reflect a mixed ancestry likely originating from outcrosses between genetically distinct lineages (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on genomic data, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Mosaic strains have probably arisen as result of human activities.
source: Mosaic strains have probably arisen as result of human activities (Liti et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Liti et al., 2009.

claim: Clinical isolates and those used in bakeries and in the laboratory tend to be mosaics.
source: Clinical isolates and those used in bakeries and in the laboratory tend to be mosaics, and most of their genomes can be traced to already characterized genetically distinct lineages.
evidence: This is based on genomic data from sequencing studies.

claim: Most of the genomes of mosaic strains can be traced to already characterized genetically distinct lineages.
source: Clinical isolates and those used in bakeries and in the laboratory tend to be mosaics, and most of their genomes can be traced to already characterized genetically distinct lineages.
evidence: This is based on genomic data from sequencing studies.

claim: Future population genomics studies should further define the genomic features of S. cerevisiae and allow the hybridisation events that generated mosaic strains to be reconstructed.
source: Future population genomics studies should further define the genomic features of S. cerevisiae and allow the hybridisation events that generated these mosaic strains to be reconstructed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research.

claim: Recent insights into the natural history of S. cerevisiae have shown that the reference lab strains represent only a subset of the many aspects of natural yeast life.
source: Recent insights into the natural history of S. cerevisiae have shown that the reference lab strains represent only a subset of the many aspects of natural yeast life.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings from recent studies.

claim: Population genomics offer a powerful approach, termed 'reverse ecology', to investigate the natural history of the species.
source: Population genomics offer a powerful approach, termed 'reverse ecology' (Li et al., 2008), to investigate the natural history of the species.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: Population-level sequencing applied to thousands of strains will further illuminate the natural history of S. cerevisiae.
source: Population-level sequencing applied to thousands of strains will further illuminate the natural history of S. cerevisiae, and the genomes of highly diverged lineages that predate domestication will reveal the impact of human activity on the species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research.

claim: The genomes of highly diverged lineages that predate domestication will reveal the impact of human activity on the species.
source: Population-level sequencing applied to thousands of strains will further illuminate the natural history of S. cerevisiae, and the genomes of highly diverged lineages that predate domestication will reveal the impact of human activity on the species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research.

claim: Analysing large numbers of strains offers the opportunity to directly test associations between genotype and phenotype.
source: Analysing large numbers of strains also offers the opportunity to directly test associations between genotype and phenotype.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of large-scale genomic studies.

claim: Some lineages have specific genomic signatures that underlie phenotypes.
source: Some lineages have specific genomic signatures that underlie phenotypes (Skelly et al., 2013) but whether this is driven by adaptation or by genetic drift remains an open question (Warringer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skelly et al., 2013.

claim: Whether genomic signatures underlying phenotypes are driven by adaptation or by genetic drift remains an open question.
source: Some lineages have specific genomic signatures that underlie phenotypes (Skelly et al., 2013) but whether this is driven by adaptation or by genetic drift remains an open question (Warringer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Warringer et al., 2011.

claim: Genotype-phenotype associations are not restricted to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) but can extend to genome content, copy number, ploidy and structural variation.
source: Genotype-phenotype associations are not restricted to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) but can extend to genome content, copy number, ploidy and structural variation (Box 1).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about genomic variation.

claim: Recent reports have shown that accessory genes vary between lineages and constitute a large fraction of genome variation between individuals.
source: Recent reports have shown that accessory genes vary between lineages and constitute a large fraction of genome variation between individuals (Bergström et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bergström et al., 2014.

claim: Certain forms of non-genetic variation, such as prions, might be important determinants of phenotypic variation.
source: Certain forms of non-genetic variation, such as prions, might also be important determinants of phenotypic variation (Jarosz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jarosz et al., 2014.

claim: Artificial populations of recombinant strains are now available, including a multi-parent population derived from highly diverged lineages.
source: Artificial populations of recombinant strains are now available, including a multi-parent population derived from highly diverged lineages (Cubillos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cubillos et al., 2013.

claim: Multi-parent populations promise to bring yeast to the forefront of complex trait analysis together with other model systems where multi-parent populations are already established.
source: These approaches promise to bring yeast to the forefront of complex trait analysis together with other model systems where multi-parent populations are already established (Kover et al., 2009; Aylor et al., 2011; King et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to Kover et al., 2009; Aylor et al., 2011; King et al., 2012.

claim: A better knowledge of the natural history of S. cerevisiae is essential for interpreting its biology.
source: In summary, a better knowledge of the natural history of this species is essential for interpreting its biology.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of natural history knowledge.

claim: Identifying how the S. cerevisiae life cycle progresses in the wild will allow better understanding of the genetic and environmental factors that are relevant to its fitness.
source: Identifying how the S. cerevisiae life cycle progresses in the wild will allow us to better understand the genetic and environmental factors that are relevant to its fitness (Box 1).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research.

claim: Yeast fitness has been largely approximated to mitotic growth, which disregards mortality during periods that do not support reproduction.
source: Yeast fitness has been largely approximated to mitotic growth, which disregards mortality during periods that do not support reproduction.
evidence: This is a critical observation about current research practices.

claim: It is likely that yeasts in nature spend most of their chronological life in a non-dividing state.
source: However, it is likely that yeasts in nature spend most of their chronological life in a non-dividing state.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological considerations.

claim: The ability to survive in a non-dividing state is probably exposed to strong selection.
source: The ability to survive in that state is therefore probably exposed to strong selection.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Measuring the impact of natural genetic variation on longevity related traits might be crucial for understanding the selective pressures that yeasts are exposed to during their life cycle.
source: Thus, measuring the impact of natural genetic variation on longevity related traits might be crucial for understanding the selective pressures that yeasts are exposed to during their life cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Sporulation, spore viability and germination time are complex traits and strongly affected by the environment.
source: Consideration must also be given to other aspects of the life cycle, such as sporulation, spore viability and germination time, each of which are also complex traits and strongly affected by the environment.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: Exploiting the natural variation of S. cerevisiae and its close relatives using genomics methodologies is enabling a new era of functional and evolutionary genetics studies of this classic model organism.
source: Exploiting the natural variation of S. cerevisiae and its close relatives using genomics methodologies is enabling a new era of functional and evolutionary genetics studies of this classic model organism (Nieduszynski and Liti, 2011; Fay, 2013; Lehner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nieduszynski and Liti, 2011; Fay, 2013; Lehner, 2013.

claim: Figure 1A shows budding cells of the reference (S288c) strain of S. cerevisiae, expressing red fluorescent protein (RFP), which marks the centre of the cell, stained with calcofluor-white, which stains the outer walls of the cells blue.
source: (A) Budding cells of the reference (S288c) strain of S. cerevisiae, expressing red fluorescent protein (RFP), which marks the centre of the cell. The cells are also stained with calcofluor-white, which stains the outer walls of the cells blue.
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1A.

claim: Figure 1B shows sporulating cells of the North American oak S. cerevisiae isolate YPS606, stained with calcofluor-white, in which the protein SPS2 is labelled with GFP, which marks the ascospore wall in green.
source: (B) Sporulating cells of the North American oak S. cerevisiae isolate YPS606, stained with calcofluor-white, in which the protein SPS2 is labelled with GFP (Gerke et al., 2006), which marks the ascospore wall in green.
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1B, supported by citation to Gerke et al., 2006.

claim: Figure 1C shows a clonal colony with a population size of approximately 7 × 10^6 cells derived from a single S. cerevisiae cell grown on a solid agar medium.
source: (C) A clonal colony with a population size of approximately 7 × 106 cells derived from a single S. cerevisiae cell grown on a solid agar medium.
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1C.

claim: Colony structures like those shown in Figure 1C have never been observed in the wild.
source: Such colony structures have never been observed in the wild.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1.

claim: Figure 2A shows a close-up of a fermenting bertam palm bud from which the Malaysian S. cerevisiae lineage has been isolated.
source: (A) A close-up of a fermenting bertam palm bud; the Malaysian S. cerevisiae lineage has been isolated from these palms (Wiens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 2A, supported by citation to Wiens et al., 2008.

claim: Figure 2B shows a primeval rainforest in the tropical highland of Hainan where the highly diverged Chinese lineages (CHN-I, CHN-III and CHN-V) have been isolated.
source: (B) A primeval rainforest in the tropical highland of Hainan where the highly diverged Chinese lineages (CHN-I, CHN-III and CHN-V) have been isolated (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 2B, supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Lineages CHN-I, CHN-III, CHN-V were mostly isolated from Fagaceae trees in the rainforest of the tropical Hainan Island in the South China Sea.
source: Lineages CHN-I, CHN-III, CHN-V were mostly isolated from Fagaceae trees in the rainforest of the tropical Hainan Island in the South China Sea.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3A.

claim: Lineages CHN-II and CHN-IV were isolated from temperate areas in north China (Shaanxi province and Beijing province, respectively).
source: Lineages CHN-II and CHN-IV were isolated from temperate areas in north China (Shaanxi province and Beijing province, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3A.

claim: The genomes of both Y55 and SK1 are mostly derived from the West African lineage.
source: The genomes of both Y55 and SK1 are mostly derived from the West African lineage (red line).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3B and shown in the figure.

claim: Y55 has three segments (0–50 kb, around 400 kb, from 650 kb to the right telomere) with high similarity to the Wine/European genome.
source: Y55 has three segments (0–50 kb, around 400 kb, from 650 kb to the right telomere) with high similarity to the Wine/European genome (yellow line).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3B and shown in the figure.

claim: SK1 has a large segment (650–750 kb) with higher similarity to the Sake lineage.
source: Likewise, SK1 has a large segment (650–750 kb) with higher similarity to the Sake lineage (light green line).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3B and shown in the figure.

claim: The analysis shown in Figure 3B has revealed the mosaic genome structure of many S. cerevisiae isolates.
source: This type of analysis has revealed the mosaic genome structure of many S. cerevisiae isolates (Liti et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3B, supported by citation to Liti et al., 2009.
